title: Carry-On Only: The Packing System That Fits Two Weeks in One Bag
metaDescription: A practical carry-on packing method — what to bring, what to leave, how to handle liquids and laundry, and the rules that make one bag work for any trip length.
excerpt: Trip length has almost nothing to do with how much you need to pack. Here is the system that makes one bag work for two weeks.
author: Travel Editors
content:
The single most transformative change you can make to how you travel is not a destination or a booking tactic. It is carrying less.

Hand luggage only means no check-in queue, no baggage carousel, no lost luggage, no baggage fee, and the ability to walk out of an airport and onto a train twenty minutes after landing. On a short trip it saves you hours. On a long one it changes what kind of travel is possible.

The objection is always the same: *two weeks in one bag?* Yes. Because the amount you need has very little to do with how long you are going.

## The Insight That Makes It Work

**Packing scales with laundry frequency, not trip length.**

If you do laundry once a week, a two-week trip needs exactly the same clothes as a one-week trip. A four-week trip needs the same again. The only things that scale with duration are consumables, and those can be bought anywhere.

Once you accept that, the whole problem collapses into a much smaller one: what do you need for **five to seven days**, given that you will wash things?

## The Core Wardrobe

For a week between laundries, in a moderate climate:

- **4–5 tops** — a mix of short and long sleeve
- **2 bottoms** — one you travel in, one spare. Three if one is a pair of shorts
- **1 outer layer** — a light insulating layer appropriate to the climate
- **1 waterproof shell** — packable, genuinely waterproof
- **5–7 pairs of underwear and socks** — the only category worth packing generously, because they are small and matter
- **2 pairs of shoes maximum**, one of which is on your feet
- **1 dressier item** if your trip needs one — a shirt, a dress
- **Swimwear** if relevant

That is it. It fits in a 40-litre bag with room to spare.

![Packing travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1682687220742-aba13b6e50ba?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## The Rules Behind the List

**One colour palette.** Choose a base — black, navy, olive, grey — and make everything work with everything. This is the trick that makes four tops feel like eight outfits, and it is the difference between a functional packing list and a suitcase of orphaned items.

**Shoes are the constraint.** They are the heaviest, bulkiest thing you own. Two pairs, maximum, and one is worn in transit. Wear the heaviest pair on the plane. A third pair "just in case" is the most common packing mistake there is.

**Merino wool earns its cost.** It resists odour in a way cotton does not — a merino t-shirt can be worn three or four days before it needs washing, and it dries overnight. Two merino tops replace five cotton ones. It is expensive and it is the highest-return purchase in travel gear.

**Cotton is the enemy on a long trip.** It is heavy, it holds odour, and it takes a full day to dry. Synthetics and merino dry in hours.

**Layers, not bulk.** Three thin layers are warmer, more versatile and more packable than one thick one.

**If you are not sure, leave it.** The universal rule. The item you hesitated over is the item you will not wear. You can buy almost anything almost anywhere, and buying a jumper in Oslo because you got the forecast wrong is a better outcome than carrying one for three weeks you did not need.

## Liquids and Toiletries

The limits: containers of **100ml or less**, all fitting in a single clear resealable bag of roughly one litre, one bag per passenger. Many airports are upgrading to scanners that relax this, but the rollout is uneven and the old rule still applies at most.

How to stay inside it comfortably:

- **Solid alternatives.** Shampoo bars, conditioner bars, solid deodorant, toothpaste tablets. None of these count as liquids, and they free up the entire bag for the things that must be liquid.
- **Decant.** You do not need a full bottle for two weeks. Small refillable bottles solve most of it.
- **Buy at the destination.** Sunscreen, shower gel and toothpaste are available everywhere and are heavy. Buy on arrival.
- **Medication is exempt** from the liquid limit in most jurisdictions when it is prescribed, but carry it in original packaging with the prescription.

![Packing travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1519055548599-6d4d129508c4?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Doing Laundry on the Road

This is the part people imagine as a burden and is actually trivial.

- **Sink washing.** A t-shirt, socks and underwear take five minutes in a sink with a small tube of travel detergent. Roll in a towel to wring out, hang overnight. Merino and synthetics are dry by morning.
- **Laundromats and laundry services.** In most of Asia and Latin America, a laundry service costs very little per kilo and returns things folded within a day. This is cheaper and faster than doing it yourself.
- **Accommodation with a washing machine.** On any trip longer than ten days, this is worth prioritising over almost any other amenity. It is the difference between packing for one week and packing for three.
- **A universal sink plug and a length of cord.** Tiny, weightless, and they solve the two problems that make sink laundry annoying.

## Packing the Bag

- **Roll rather than fold** for most things — it compresses better and creases less.
- **Packing cubes** genuinely help, less for compression than for organisation. Three cubes — tops, bottoms, underwear — mean you never unpack the whole bag to find one thing.
- **Heavy items low and against your back** if it is a backpack, for balance.
- **Electronics and liquids on top** or in an outer pocket, so security checks do not require dismantling everything.
- **Wear the bulk.** Jacket, boots and the heaviest layer go on your body in transit, not in the bag.

## What to Actually Bring Beyond Clothes

- **A power bank**, charged. An uncharged one is dead weight
- **A universal adapter** with USB ports, so one adapter serves the whole group
- **One cable per device**, plus one spare
- **A small medical kit** — painkillers, plasters, rehydration salts, anti-diarrhoeal, motion sickness tablets, and any personal medication with a few extra days' buffer
- **A packable day bag** for daily use, so your main bag stays at the accommodation
- **Copies of documents** — offline on your phone, plus one paper copy stored separately
- **Earplugs and an eye mask.** Small, weightless, and they protect the thing that determines whether the whole trip is enjoyable

## What to Leave

- The third pair of shoes
- The "just in case" formal outfit, unless you have a specific event
- A full-size towel, unless camping — accommodation provides them and a small quick-dry one covers the rest
- Books, beyond one. An e-reader or your phone handles the rest
- More than one bag of electronics accessories
- Anything you have not used on the last two trips

## The Honest Exceptions

Carry-on only is not universal. Genuine exceptions:

- **Ski and technical gear** — boots and hardware do not compress
- **Diving equipment**
- **Photography kit** beyond a body and one or two lenses
- **Travelling with very young children**, where the consumables genuinely scale
- **Long trips crossing extreme climate ranges** — a month spanning tropical beach and high-altitude cold is a real packing problem
- **Cabin bag charges.** On some budget airlines a large cabin bag now costs as much as a checked one, which changes the arithmetic. Check the specific allowance before assuming

Outside those, the constraint is almost always habit rather than necessity — and the first trip you take with one bag tends to be the last one you take with two.
